newsitem.title: CHINA: Sino-Europe talks on WTO yield no immediate result.
newsitem.headline: Sino-Europe talks on WTO yield no immediate result.

text.p: Chinese and European negotiators on Thursday ended four days of talks with no immediate progress on Beijing's plan to join the World Trade Organisation (WTO), European Union officials said.
Beijing's offered terms for WTO entry remained well short of requirements in the key area of trade in services, but EU officials said they were heartened by the attitude of Chinese negotiators.

"Discussions were open and constructive, even if they did not yield immediate results," the EU said in a statement that laid out in unusual detail the conditions attached by Europe to China's entry to the global trade club.

The EU was seeking commitments from China on market access for services such as telecommunications, banking, insurance, news agencies and retailing, said Gerard Depayre, EU deputy director-general for external relations.
"Access to foreign markets -- especially the Chinese market, which has significant growth potential -- is very important," Depayre told a news briefing in Beijing.

"We consider the Chinese offer at this stage was... not commensurate with the weight of China in the world economy, not commensurate with economic realities in China... and certainly not commensurate with projected new regulation," he said.
Much remained to be done to hammer out an adequate set of Chinese commitments, despite proposals from Beijing that had kick-started the stalled accession process, he said.
China's WTO offer even lagged behind current commercial realities in some markets, where foreigners were winning access on an unofficial basis, he said.
China has for years campaigned to be allowed to join the WTO and its predecessor, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, but has failed to agree on terms with existing members.
Chinese Premier Li Peng said last week the accession delays were abnormal and left an incomplete WTO lacking one of the largest and fastest-growing economies.
Beijing has campaigned for the favourable conditions accorded other developing countries, but some Western nations have argued that the booming Chinese economy is too big to be treated so leniently.

The Beijing talks had dealt extensively with European demands for improved access to China's markets for banking services, insurance, securities trading, maritime shipping including dredging and telecommunications, Depayre said.

Brussels expected Chinese commitments to gradually allow foreign banking and insurance services to be offered to local consumers, entry for foreign securities companies and eased restrictions on foreign law firms, he said.

China should allow unrestricted establishment of shipping companies, the setting up of foreign wholesale and retail firms, establishment rights for news and travel agencies, he said. He declined to give details of EU demands or expected timetables.
EU officials also called for the tightly guarded but fast-growing telecommunications sector to be opened to foreign competition -- a demand Beijing has rejected in the past.
China was already a major player in worldwide shipping, making it difficult to justify the restrictions Beijing forced on foreign companies, Depayre said.
Premier Li last week reaffirmed Beijing's enthusiasm for WTO entry, despite condemning delays as abnormal.
"China is a major trading country and would very much like to join this organisation," Li said. "Not only does the WTO need China, but China also needs the WTO."
